---
title: "Risks, blocked work and changing plans"
last-reviewed: "2026-08-31"
---

Not every delay is the same problem. Waiting for an approval, discovering an infeasible method and facing an uncertain risk require different responses. If you label all of them “blocked,” the next action stays vague. Classify what has happened, identify the decision-maker and record the smallest consequence that matters. Some work can continue around the blockage; some requires a formal change; some must stop until authority or safety is restored.

## Name what has happened

Name the state accurately, record its consequence and give it an owner, trigger and next decision. A risk needs prevention and contingency. An issue needs response. Waiting needs a follow-up threshold. Blocked work needs another route or escalation. A material change needs an impact review and the required approval before affected work proceeds.

The aim is not to keep a perfect register. It is to make uncertainty visible early enough to protect participants, evidence, people and time.

| State | Meaning | Immediate response |
|---|---|---|
| Risk | an uncertain event or condition that could affect the project | reduce likelihood or consequence; define a trigger and contingency |
| Issue | the event has happened or the condition already exists | contain harm, establish facts, assign response and decide |
| Waiting | progress depends on a known external action or event | record requester, request date, promised response and follow-up threshold |
| Blocked | the current route cannot produce the required outcome | identify the blocker, affected milestone, alternatives and escalation point |
| Incident | harm, breach, unsafe conduct or loss may have occurred | preserve evidence and use the authorised urgent reporting route |
| Change | an accepted alteration to a baseline question, method, protocol, scope, role, resource, schedule or output | assess downstream effects, obtain required authority and update linked records |

A single situation may move through several states. “Data access may be delayed” is a risk. Once the promised decision is overdue it is an issue. Work may be waiting on the custodian without being blocked if analysis preparation can continue. It becomes blocked when no available work can produce the milestone. A decision to use another dataset is a proposed change, not an automatic fix.

Do not use “blocked” to mean difficult, unpleasant or not yet scheduled. Do not use “waiting” to hide a decision that nobody has taken ownership of.

## Write the risk so someone can act on it

A usable risk statement connects cause, event and consequence:

> Because access depends on a partner's legal review, the de-identified extract may not arrive before the analysis window, which could make the primary study infeasible within candidature.

That is more actionable than “data access: high risk”. Record:

- the evidence currently available;
- the consequence and who or what may be affected;
- likelihood and consequence only to the precision the evidence supports;
- prevention or mitigation;
- contingency if the event occurs;
- owner of each action;
- a dated trigger for review or activation;
- current state; and
- closure evidence.

Numbers and red–amber–green labels can create false precision. Use them only when the team shares definitions. A plain description of consequence, urgency and uncertainty is often clearer.

## Decide the fallback before you need it

A contingency is the route you will take if a named trigger occurs. Writing “find another method” does not count. By the time a trigger is reached, you may have less time, fewer options and more pressure to protect work already done.

For each risk that could threaten a study, milestone or duty of care, record:

1. **What you are protecting:** the research question, participant obligation, irreplaceable material, milestone or other outcome that matters.
2. **The trigger:** an observable event, threshold or date that prompts a decision.
3. **The fallback:** a route that is feasible enough to test now, not a hopeful sentence written for a form.
4. **Who decides:** the person who can activate the fallback, plus any ethics, governance, data, safety or candidature authority required.
5. **What must be ready:** approval, access, skills, code, equipment, budget or another prerequisite.
6. **The review date:** when you will check whether the trigger, fallback or protected outcome has changed.
7. **Proof that the switch worked:** the record, test or approval that shows the alternative is usable.

Official research-funding guidance treats uncertainty as part of research planning and asks applicants to identify alternative approaches, not merely rate the original plan [@ukri-stfc-case-contingency-2022]. Broader risk guidance also supports named owners, agreed triggers, monitoring and contingency arrangements [@hm-treasury-orange-book-2026]. These sources come from particular UK systems. The useful general lesson is to decide what will prompt action, who can decide and what must remain protected; they do not set the rules for your candidature.

Run a cheap test while the first route is still available. Check whether the alternative dataset contains the required variables. Rehearse a restore. Ask whether another supervisor can cover the decisions due during an absence. Fit the proposed backup analysis to simulated data and state which claim it could support. A fallback that has never been checked is another uncertainty, not yet a plan.

## Keep the non-negotiables in place

A fallback may change the route, but it cannot quietly remove the conditions that made the research acceptable. Before activation, check whether it changes:

- who can be approached and how consent is obtained;
- participant burden, welfare, safety or withdrawal arrangements;
- approved sites, populations, procedures, data or purposes;
- privacy, confidentiality, cultural governance or data access;
- the skills, training or authorisation required to do the work safely;
- the analysis, registration or claim the study was designed to support; or
- an agreement with a partner, funder or institution.

If it does, pause the affected work until the responsible authority has decided whether an amendment, notification, new permission or another formal step is required. In Australian human research, the National Statement governs ethical review and approved conduct; the exact process still depends on the institution and project [@national-statement-2025]. Australian data guidance likewise keeps storage, access, retention and disposal duties attached to the research when plans change [@nhmrc-data-guide].

Research-continuity guidance makes the same practical point for disrupted teams: alternative personnel need the right skills, approval and access, while participant obligations, safety and data controls continue [@cornell-research-continuity].

## Prepare for the disruptions that recur

The examples below are starting points. Replace the sample triggers with thresholds that fit the method, remaining time and governing rules.

| Disruption | Useful trigger | What to prepare before the trigger | If the trigger is reached |
|---|---|---|---|
| Data or site access is delayed | written access, variable availability or site permission is not confirmed by the last date that preserves the analysis window | test an authorised public or already-held source; identify the narrower question it could answer | take the access evidence and tested alternative to the relevant scientific, data and candidature decision-makers |
| Recruitment falls short | eligible approaches, enrolments or retention fall below a prespecified rate at a dated review | verify the pool and route; identify approved ways to reduce burden or add sites; define the smallest still-informative design | do not relax eligibility, consent or contact rules informally; seek method and ethics advice on amendment, redesign, bounded analysis or stopping |
| Equipment fails or data are lost | calibration fails, downtime exceeds the buffer, or the authoritative copy cannot be restored | rehearse restore; retain calibration and maintenance records; check access to a suitable alternative instrument or service | protect remaining material, record the incident and test comparability before combining or replacing measurements |
| A supervisor is unavailable | a planned absence overlaps a decision gate, or minimum contact and decision coverage cannot be maintained | name the alternative contact; keep decisions, methods and next actions readable by the supervisory team | activate local continuity arrangements and seek formal replacement or additional supervision when required |
| An analysis assumption fails | a prespecified diagnostic or data condition shows the planned analysis cannot support the intended claim | identify a defensible alternative analysis or narrower claim and decide how deviations will be recorded | consult the relevant method specialist; preserve the original plan; label exploratory work and update the claim rather than searching for a favourable result |
| Personal circumstances reduce capacity | health, disability, caring, financial or other disruption makes the current workload, safety or deadline unworkable | know the confidential support and candidature routes; keep records understandable so work can pause or be handed over safely | protect immediate wellbeing and essential duties, then seek leave, adjustment, workload or timeline decisions through the authorised route; keep personal details out of the project register |
| The timeline is compressed | the critical path plus a realistic correction buffer no longer fits the time remaining | rank studies and outputs by contribution; identify work that can be narrowed, reordered or removed without misrepresentation | re-plan the contribution and seek any formal extension or scope decision; do not recover time by skipping consent, quality checks, data controls or honest reporting |

Recruitment deserves an early trigger rather than a late surprise. In a systematic review of 347 randomised trials approved in four countries, 31.1% were discontinued and poor recruitment was the most common reported reason. Those figures apply to the reviewed clinical trials, not to every doctoral study, but they show why recruitment assumptions should be checked while a redesign is still possible [@speich-2025-trial-discontinuation].

Supervision continuity is partly an institutional responsibility. Australian guidance expects institutions to support alternative arrangements when personnel changes make existing supervision untenable [@nhmrc-supervision-guide-2019]. UK guidance similarly recommends a known alternative contact and continued supervision when a main supervisor is absent [@qaa-research-degrees-2018]. Ask what your own institution provides before an absence becomes a crisis.

## Choose how to respond

For an ordinary project risk, consider whether to:

- **avoid** it by changing the route before exposure;
- **reduce** its likelihood or consequence;
- **share or transfer** a bounded responsibility to someone with authority or capability;
- **accept** it explicitly with a trigger and contingency; or
- **escalate** because the consequence or authority exceeds the team's remit.

Acceptance does not mean ignoring a risk. It means recording why further control is disproportionate, who accepted the residual exposure and when that decision will be reviewed.

Immediate safety, integrity, privacy, participant-welfare or legal concerns do not wait for an ordinary weekly review. Use the relevant urgent local process and do not investigate beyond your authority.

## Put a date on waiting

Every external dependency should have:

1. a specific request and named recipient;
2. the date sent and evidence of receipt if consequential;
3. the expected response or decision;
4. an agreed or reasonable follow-up date;
5. work that can proceed safely meanwhile;
6. an alternative or contingency; and
7. an escalation threshold.

“Waiting for ethics” is too vague. Record whether the application was submitted, administratively accepted, under review, returned for changes or approved. Those states have different implications. Never describe submission as approval.

## Find the exact blocker

Use four questions:

1. **Required outcome:** What evidence or decision cannot currently be produced?
2. **Constraint:** What exactly prevents the current route from producing it?
3. **Control:** Which part can the student, team, collaborator or institution change?
4. **Threshold:** By when must an alternative or formal change be chosen?

Then identify parallel work that remains legitimate. Preparing code against synthetic data may reduce later delay; collecting unapproved real data does not. Repeatedly polishing unrelated prose may create activity without protecting the threatened milestone.

::: {.decision-card}
**Smallest useful next action:** Write one sentence naming the blocked outcome, the constraint, its owner and the date at which the current route becomes untenable. Then take that sentence to the person with authority to decide among realistic options.
:::

## Record why the plan changed

A baseline is the last accepted version of the relevant plan: research question, protocol, analysis plan, ethics application, data-management plan, authorship understanding, milestone or output scope. A change request explains why that baseline should change and what else the change affects.

Before implementing a material change, assess:

| Domain | Questions |
|---|---|
| Research question and contribution | Does the revised work answer the same question? Is the intended contribution narrower or different? |
| Design and inference | Do sampling, measurement, comparison, analysis and claims still align? |
| Ethics, governance and safety | Is an amendment, notification, new permission or safety review required before work? |
| Data and code | Do schemas, provenance, access, validation, scripts and reproducibility records change? |
| People and commitments | Are participants, partners, collaborators, workload, authorship or ownership affected? |
| Time and resources | Which milestones, dependencies, buffers, costs and opportunity costs change? |
| Outputs | Which chapters, registrations, manuscripts, reports or communications must be revised? |
| Authority | Who can recommend, approve, implement and verify the change? |

Record the current baseline, precipitating evidence, realistic options, recommendation, impact analysis, required approvals, decision, implementation owner and verification evidence. Link the change to the decision log rather than silently replacing old files.

Small reversible adjustments do not need elaborate paperwork. The record should be proportionate to the consequence and reversibility. A change affecting participant-facing material, consent, approved data use, safety, registered analysis or contractual commitments may be consequential even if it takes only minutes to edit.

## Example: access has not arrived

**Baseline:** The primary study uses a partner-controlled dataset. Written access confirmation was required by 15 September so analysis could begin in October.

**Current evidence:** The custodian acknowledged the request but legal review has no decision date. The trigger has passed. No data have been transferred.

**Classification:** The possible delay was a risk; the missed confirmation is now an issue. The primary analysis is waiting and will become blocked at the latest feasible start date.

**Options:**

1. continue waiting with a final decision date and protect the buffer;
2. narrow the original study to variables already authorised;
3. activate a public-data alternative answering a bounded version of the question;
4. reorder linked studies while retaining the access route; or
5. pause or remove the study through the formal candidature process.

**Cheap tests:** Obtain a written variable list and decision timetable; run the planned pipeline against synthetic data; assess whether the alternative dataset can support the same inference; map effects on ethics, contribution and milestones.

**Recommendation:** Continue preparation only until the named decision date while testing the public-data alternative. If access remains unconfirmed, submit a documented change recommendation rather than spending the remaining buffer on repeated informal follow-up.

**Authority boundary:** The student can prepare options and tests. The custodian controls access. Supervisors can recommend a scientific route. Ethics, governance and candidature authorities decide changes within their remit.

**Evidence of completion:** A dated decision, any required approval, revised question and method records, updated milestones and risk status, and a reproducible record showing which dataset and analysis route became authoritative.

## How waiting turns into unmanaged drift

- keeping risks in someone's memory rather than a shared recoverable record;
- listing a risk without a trigger, owner or contingency;
- using “high risk” without stating the consequence;
- copying unresolved items forward at every meeting;
- treating an unanswered request as permission;
- calling work blocked without identifying the required outcome;
- escalating a vague complaint instead of a decision-ready problem;
- implementing a material change before required approval;
- updating the protocol but not the ethics, data, code, milestone or authorship records;
- preserving the deadline by quietly weakening the inference;
- treating sunk effort as a reason to continue an untenable route; and
- hiding bad news until no feasible alternative remains.

## Check that the response fits the risk

Risk and change control are usable when consequential uncertainties and current problems are distinguished; every live item has an owner and next decision point; waiting has a follow-up threshold; blockers identify the affected outcome and alternatives; material changes have an impact analysis and authority path; and closure is supported by evidence rather than disappearance from a list.

## Take a clear account of the problem

Bring:

- a one-sentence classification and consequence;
- the relevant baseline and current evidence;
- the trigger already reached or approaching;
- actions already taken and their results;
- two or more feasible options, including their trade-offs;
- your provisional recommendation;
- approvals or specialist advice that may be required; and
- one precise decision request with a date.

## Check the consequence before changing course

- [ ] The item is classified as risk, issue, waiting, blocked, incident or proposed change.
- [ ] The affected outcome and consequence are explicit.
- [ ] Facts, assumptions and missing evidence are separated.
- [ ] Each response has an owner and dated trigger.
- [ ] Waiting work has a follow-up and escalation threshold.
- [ ] A contingency can be activated before the critical buffer is exhausted.
- [ ] Proposed changes are checked across question, design, ethics, data, people, time and outputs.
- [ ] Required authority is identified before affected work proceeds.
- [ ] Accepted changes update all linked records.
- [ ] Closure requires observable evidence.

## Sources and limits

The risk-state and change-impact framework is an editorial decision aid. The contingency fields draw on official research-funder, public-sector risk and university continuity guidance [@ukri-stfc-case-contingency-2022; @hm-treasury-orange-book-2026; @cornell-research-continuity]. Those sources support general planning practices; they do not set doctoral rules. The Australian Code, National Statement, data-management guide and supervision guide support the authority, participant, data and supervision boundaries used here [@australian-code-2018; @national-statement-2025; @nhmrc-data-guide; @nhmrc-supervision-guide-2019]. Other jurisdictions and local processes differ. The recruitment statistic is evidence from clinical randomised trials, not an estimate for graduate research as a whole [@speich-2025-trial-discontinuation].
